content:
Earlier this year, when Apple launched the MacBook Neo, the personal computer market was caught completely off guard. Although the aggressive pricing strategy of that laptop has since been forced to adjust in response to market conditions, it has taken several months before we have seen competitors running Windows successively announce their own competing products. Now it is HP's turn to take the stage today — the company has unveiled a new laptop equipped with an OLED display, with pricing also starting from US$699, but there are quite a few conditions attached.

The top-rated comment was posted by TurboFool.

Lately there has been a flood of Windows news that has absolutely nothing to do with Google, which is a cause for concern. Some of it is only tangentially related to Google — at best it is an ARM device, or could loosely be considered a cousin of an Android device, but that is already a rather strained argument. However, this is an x86-based Windows laptop, and there is no justification at all for including it here. I migrated here from sites like AP and AA, and I watched those platforms gradually fill up with off-topic content just to pad post counts, which worries me greatly. I really cannot bear to lose another one.

The overall design of the HP OmniBook 5 14 looks like a budget, colourful version of the MacBook Neo — a cross between the more refined muted greens and blues of the iPad Air lineup. At just 11.77mm thick and packing a 14-inch display while weighing only 2.56 pounds, it would have been a perfect fit for the back-to-school shopping season, but HP appears to have missed the optimal timing. That said, the 14-inch display is the biggest highlight of this laptop — it ditches the IPS panels common at this price point in favour of one of two OLED options, more on which later. The sides of the chassis come with two full-function USB-C ports and a headphone jack, and when you open the lid, an FHD camera supporting Windows Hello greets you.

On the hardware specs front, HP says it supports up to an Intel Core 7 processor, but the model currently being shown is the only option available. Battery life looks impressive on paper — up to 42 hours of local video playback — but the battery capacity has not been disclosed, and it has to be said that local video playback tests do not necessarily reflect real-world usage. HP says the device is compatible with the company's 65W mini GaN charger, and I would expect the charger to be included in the box. Beyond that, dual microphones and audio tuned by Poly Studio are all we know in terms of specs. If you feel there is still a lot of information missing, you are not alone.

To begin with, it remains unclear which processor the US$700 version of the laptop will use, making it hard to compare against Apple's A18 Pro. HP has also chosen not to disclose any storage or memory configurations — not even an "up to" figure — which is a clear reflection of just how brutally the PC market is being squeezed amid the current memory shortage. Even the headline feature of this laptop comes with a major caveat; HP spent a great deal of its announcement talking up the 2.5K OLED display, but that version will not ship until March 2027. The version going on sale at Best Buy later this month will come with a 2K OLED display, with brightness dropping sharply from 650 nits to a mere 300 nits.

Many questions remain unanswered, and some of the answers are underwhelming, but if you are still interested in this HP laptop, stay tuned for more details to be revealed before it officially goes on sale.
